counter_evidence:
I ran the claim's own falsification test on this box, with Node 24.22.1 and libuv 1.52.1, on local NTFS under the session scratchpad. Each writer used writeFileSync(tmp) then renameSync(tmp, events/<aa>/<sha>.json), 8 processes x 1,000 events. Results are in C:\Users\User\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-User-Documents-projects-EMS-workshop1--claude-worktrees-knowledge-store-research-9c609c\f3bbe503-2a20-4258-976b-7d457d3bf63a\scratchpad\ksc3-ops-r9d41\runs\naive-same.log, batch1.log, batch2.log and batch3.log.

(1) Identical events, same order: 99 rename EPERM (errno -4048, syscall rename, destination already existed) and 99 leftover .tmp-<pid> files. A repeat gave 104/104. With 2 concurrent reader processes it gave 84/84. A variant that unlinks the temp file in its catch block left 0 temp files but still threw 126 EPERM.

(2) The same 1,000 events in a different shuffled order per process: 4 EPERM and 4 leftover temp files. A repeat with 2 readers gave 2/2.

(3) 500 shared plus 500 unique events per process: 2 EPERM and 2 leftover temp files.

(4) Unique events only: 0 errors and 0 leftover temp files, with or without readers. So the failure is specific to renaming over an existing file. That is exactly the identical-event case the claim includes.

Deterministic mechanism (holdopen.log): while another process holds the destination open read-only, renameSync(tmp, dest) fails with EPERM and the temp file stays. libuv opens that handle with FILE_SHARE_DELETE, and the rename still fails. Once the handle is released the same rename succeeds. Holding the source file open does not block the rename. In the store design, the destination is held open by every freshness ingest, every git add and any AV scan.

Primary sources:
- libuv src/win/fs.c: fs__rename is a bare MoveFileExW(..., MOVEFILE_REPLACE_EXISTING), with no POSIX-semantics flag and no retry.
- Microsoft's MoveFileExW page makes no atomicity guarantee. It points to MoveFileTransacted for a transacted operation.
- graceful-fs 4.2.11 polyfills.js lines 87-123, read from C:/Users/User/Documents/projects/EMS_workshop1/node_modules: on win32 it retries EACCES/EPERM/EBUSY renames for up to 60 s, but only while stat(to) returns ENOENT. Once the destination exists it returns the error. Prior art treats rename-over-existing EPERM as non-retryable.
- write-file-atomic 4.0.2 (technician-app/node_modules) serialises writes to the same target, but only inside one process (activeFiles).

The claim's support does not measure it. Proposal D's test (scratchpad archD/race.cjs) catches the rename error. If the destination exists with the same hash, it removes the temp file and counts ok++ and retried++. Its errs counter therefore counts only unabsorbed failures, so "0 errors" holds by construction for identical events. Its own design text says renameSync 'replaces an identical existing file', which my runs contradict.

The premise is also wrong for this box. Get-MpComputerStatus reports Defender AMRunningMode 'Not running'. SecurityCenter2 lists 360 Total Security with productState 331776 (0x051000, scanner on), so 360 is the active real-time scanner. Its share of the same-name races was not isolated.

The one part of the claim that held: in every run, every final file's sha256 equalled its name (bad=0). Readers made 875,027 reads with 0 hash mismatches and 0 read errors.
narrowed_claim:
This replaces the refuted claim; it is not the claim narrowed. On NTFS on this box, concurrent writers of uniquely named events through temp-then-rename produced no errors and no leftover temp files. Whenever the rename completed, the file's content hash equalled its name (0 mismatches across all runs and 875k concurrent reads).

Writing an event that already exists, by rename-over-existing, is NOT safe. It throws EPERM whenever the destination is open in another process or being replaced concurrently, and a naive writer leaves the temp file behind.

Two writer protocols showed 0 residual errors, 0 temp files and 0 bad files under 8 and 16 processes with readers:
(a) linkSync(tmp, final), which never replaces. On EEXIST, verify the existing file's sha256, then unlink the temp file. Results: 7,000 and 15,000 EEXIST absorbed; it also stays clean when the destination is held open.
(b) renameSync with EPERM/EACCES/EBUSY absorbed only when the destination exists with the matching sha256, the temp file always unlinked, and fail closed otherwise. Results: 98 to 800 EPERM absorbed per run.

On the Linux VPS, POSIX rename(2) replaces atomically. That was not tested here.
design_consequence:
1. The journal writer in K1/KS1 must not use plain temp-then-rename over an existing name. Two options:
   - Preferred: link(tmp, final) with no replace. On EEXIST, read and sha256 the existing file; equal means an idempotent success, unequal means quarantine. Then unlink the temp file in a finally block. This works on NTFS and on Linux.
   - Otherwise: rename with EPERM/EACCES/EBUSY absorbed only when the destination's sha256 matches. Any other failure gets a bounded retry and then fails closed.
   A pre-check that skips the write when the file exists does not remove the race: 1,598 EPERM were still absorbed in the skip-existing run.
2. A journal-write exception must never abort the BEGIN IMMEDIATE transaction for an event that is already durable on disk. The index insert stays INSERT OR IGNORE.
3. A crash between the write and the rename still leaves a temp file, so:
   - ingest, the freshness check and fsck accept only names matching ^[0-9a-f]{64}\.json$;
   - the store repo's .gitignore excludes *.tmp-* so a phase-close `git add` cannot commit a temp file into the journal;
   - `ks doctor`/fsck sweeps temp files older than a stated age.
4. Proposal D's LB2 evidence (archD/race.cjs) is re-labelled as non-evidence, because it masks EPERM by construction.
5. KS1's stress test must:
   - count absorbed EPERM/EEXIST separately from errors;
   - include a hold-the-destination-open case;
   - fail if the naive path is used.
6. Correct the premise "Defender is the interferer": on this box Defender is not running and 360 Total Security is the active scanner. `ks doctor` should report the AV product. Any scan exclusion for the store path is a security-setting change, so it is the owner's decision only and never part of the default install.
